## Excursion to Tulpetlac: a shrine and pilgrimage route near Mexico City

[Tulpetlac](/mexico/place/tulpetlac/) is a historic settlement in Ecatepec, State of Mexico. It is known for the Shrine of the Fifth Apparition of Our Lady of Guadalupe. According to Catholic tradition, the apparition here involved Juan Bernardino, Juan Diego's uncle, and his recovery from illness. A visit to the shrine complements an introduction to the principal Guadalupe holy sites in Mexico City.

**We have included Tulpetlac in a single standalone excursion route**, together with the archaeological site of Teotihuacan and historic Tlatelolco. This is a pilgrimage itinerary with cultural stops, rather than a separate recreational outing.

## What the current excursion includes

[Teotihuacan, Tulpetlac and Tlatelolco](/mexico/teotihuacan/teotihuacan-tulpetlac-tlatelolco-pilgrimage/) is our private excursion with an English-speaking guide and private transportation. The day begins in [Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/), with a visit to the pyramids and other ancient structures. The route then takes you to the shrine in Tulpetlac and ends at the Plaza of the Three Cultures and the Church of St. James in Tlatelolco.

The excursion includes admission to the listed attractions and **one Holy Mass along the route**. The Mass does not necessarily take place in Tulpetlac itself: the sequence of religious activities is arranged for the particular journey. Likewise, the overall itinerary does not specify the length of each individual stop.

## Why Tulpetlac matters in the history of Guadalupe

The shrine is dedicated to the Fifth Apparition of Our Lady of Guadalupe, as described in religious tradition. The place is associated with the healing of Juan Bernardino. The shrine's interior and imagery refer to Our Lady as the "Health of the Sick."

For believers, this is a place of prayer and pilgrimage. For visitors interested in cultural history, it shows how local religious traditions intertwine with architecture and everyday community life in the Valley of Mexico. Visiting the site independently is different from attending a service; visiting rules and Mass times should be checked separately.

## Teotihuacan and Tlatelolco: three distinct historical themes

[Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/) is known for the Avenue of the Dead, the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon, and the architecture of the ancient city. [Tlatelolco](/mexico/place/tlatelolco/) offers a different layering of eras: the ruins of a pre-Columbian settlement, a colonial church and modern urban buildings stand side by side.

Tulpetlac adds the Guadalupe pilgrimage theme to these two sites. The three stops should not be treated as interchangeable attractions: each has a distinct place in the narrative.

| Stop | Main theme |
|---|---|
| Teotihuacan | Ancient city |
| Tulpetlac | Guadalupe shrine |
| Tlatelolco | Three cultural eras |

If your primary goal is a religious journey, specify how much time you would like to devote to prayer and church activities before confirming the day. If archaeology matters more to you, remember that exploring the archaeological complex also takes time.

## Practical considerations for the visit

The excursion connects several sites that are far apart, so traffic around the capital needs to be taken into account. Comfortable shoes, sun protection and water are useful at the archaeological site. When visiting active places of worship, dress appropriately and respect those attending religious services.

The excursion is accompanied by an English-speaking guide. A Russian-language service, a dedicated priest, additional religious rites or special equipment are not listed among the included services. Any individual religious requirements should be discussed in advance.

## Frequently asked questions about the Tulpetlac excursion

### Can I visit Tulpetlac and Teotihuacan in a single day?

Yes. [Ada Tours' private excursion](/mexico/teotihuacan/teotihuacan-tulpetlac-tlatelolco-pilgrimage/) combines Teotihuacan, Tulpetlac and Tlatelolco in one itinerary.

### Is Holy Mass included?

The published itinerary includes one Mass along the route. Its location and time must be confirmed for the particular journey.

### Is the excursion conducted in Russian?

Russian-language guiding has not been confirmed. The current product explicitly specifies an English-speaking guide.

### Can I visit just the shrine?

An independent visit is possible under the shrine's current rules, but the Ada Tours product described here combines three stops. A separate commercial excursion solely to Tulpetlac is not offered on this page.

## Excursions and routes via Tulum: Maya ruins or arrival on the Caribbean coast

[Tulum](/mexico/place/tulum/) lies on the Caribbean coast and is known for its Maya archaeological zone above the rocky shoreline, its beaches and its tourist districts. However, in itineraries around the Yucatan Peninsula, "Tulum" may refer to **the destination for a drop-off**, rather than a guided visit to the archaeological site itself.

On our itinerary with an optional drop-off in Tulum, the main sightseeing takes place **at Chichen Itza, near a cenote and in Valladolid**. The possibility of ending the journey in Tulum town must not be confused with an included visit to the ancient ruins of Tulum.

## Confirmed itinerary with a Tulum drop-off

[Chichen Itza, a cenote and Valladolid](/mexico/chichen-itza/chichen-itza-valladolid-caribbean-transfer/) is a full-day route from Merida to the Riviera Maya. The programme includes a private transfer from your hotel in Merida, a group guided visit to [Chichen Itza](/mexico/place/chichen-itza/), a swim in a cenote, lunch and a stop in Valladolid. A private transfer then continues to one of the destinations on the Caribbean coast: Cancun, Playa del Carmen or **Tulum town**.

There is an important restriction: **transfers to the Tulum hotel zone are not provided**. This matters when choosing accommodation. If your hotel is outside the town itself, you will need to arrange the last part of the journey separately.

Guided sightseeing is provided in English and Spanish. Transportation, a guided tour of Chichen Itza, admission tickets, lunch, the cenote visit and the agreed drop-off on the Riviera Maya are included. An overnight stay is not included in the price of this excursion day.

| Route stage | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Chichen Itza | Guided sightseeing |
| Cenote | Swimming |
| Valladolid | Town stop |
| Tulum | Optional drop-off point |

## What to see in Tulum itself

Tulum's principal cultural attraction is the Maya archaeological city perched on a coastal cliff. Its historic structures and Caribbean views distinguish it from Yucatan's archaeological complexes farther inland. The archaeological zone has its own admission rules, opening hours and access conditions, published by Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH).

The wider destination also has beaches and natural attractions. Their appearance on a general page about Tulum does not mean they are visited on the "Chichen Itza, cenote and Valladolid" itinerary. Allow a separate part of your trip if you want to explore Tulum's ruins.

## When it makes sense to combine sightseeing and a transfer

The route suits travellers who are finishing the cultural part of their stay in Merida and moving to the coast. Instead of a straightforward direct transfer, the day includes several sightseeing stops. This combination takes time, however: after Chichen Itza, the cenote and Valladolid, you still need to reach your final destination.

If you also want to explore Tulum's ruins in detail that day, the schedule may be too full. It is better to plan time in the town and a separate visit to the archaeological zone.

The word "Tulum" in a list of related destinations is not enough to establish what is included. Check the programme details: where the sightseeing takes place, which admission tickets are included, precisely where the transport drops you off and whether the driver takes you to your hotel.

## Planning a visit to the ruins and beaches

Comfortable shoes, water and sun protection are useful for exploring the archaeological zone. Conservation and archaeological rules on the coast may restrict access to certain areas. Check current opening hours and admission prices against official notices for your travel date; these conditions change independently of the route from Merida to the coast.

For more time by the sea, browse [tours in Mexico](/mexico/tour/) and themed [beach holidays](/interests/beach-holidays/). This helps you plan a sightseeing transfer separately from a full day on the coast.

## Frequently asked questions about travelling via Tulum

### Does the excursion include Tulum's archaeological site?

In the [itinerary via Chichen Itza and Valladolid](/mexico/chichen-itza/chichen-itza-valladolid-caribbean-transfer/), Tulum is listed as a possible final drop-off point. A guided visit to Tulum's ruins is not confirmed as included.

### Can I be taken to a hotel in Tulum's beach zone?

The published description explicitly excludes transfers to Tulum's hotel zone. The final drop-off point and any onward transportation must be arranged in advance.

### Is a cenote included in the programme?

Yes. The cenote visit and swimming are expressly listed in the excursion. This does not mean that travellers can choose any cenote they wish.

### In what language is the excursion conducted?

English and Spanish. Other languages need to be arranged separately because they are not listed in the product description.

## Excursions to Uxmal: Maya ruins, Kabah and cenotes

[Uxmal](/mexico/place/uxmal/) is one of the major archaeological centres of Maya civilisation on the Yucatan Peninsula. Its buildings are renowned for richly decorated stone facades and the distinctive Puuc architectural style. Among its principal structures are the Pyramid of the Magician, the Governor's Palace and the Nunnery Quadrangle. Unlike Yucatan's beach destinations, Uxmal attracts visitors primarily for its history and architecture.

We offer **two excursions visiting Uxmal**. Both combine an archaeological visit with a cenote, but one focuses on Uxmal, while the other also includes Kabah. Choose according to your interest in visiting a second archaeological complex.

## Uxmal and a cenote

The [Uxmal and cenote excursion](/mexico/uxmal/uxmal-cenote-tour/) lasts 8–9 hours, with an approximate start between 9:00 and 9:30. The guide conducts the excursion in English and Spanish. The day is devoted to Uxmal's buildings and history, followed by a swim in a natural freshwater cenote.

This excursion includes shared transportation, a certified bilingual guide, and admission to Uxmal and the cenote. Meals, tips and personal expenses are not included. It suits those who want to focus on one archaeological site and finish the day relaxing by the water.

## Uxmal, Kabah and a cenote

[Uxmal, Kabah and cenote swimming](/mexico/uxmal/uxmal-kabah-cenote-tour/) also takes 8–9 hours. After Uxmal, the programme continues to [Kabah](/mexico/place/kabah/), where you can see carved facades and motifs depicting the rain god Chaac. A swim in a cenote follows.

Shared transfers, a certified bilingual guide and admission tickets to Uxmal, Kabah and the cenote are included. Meals, tips and personal expenses are excluded. This itinerary suits travellers who want to compare two centres of Puuc architecture. With the same overall duration, each site receives less time than it would on an excursion to Uxmal alone.

| Criterion | Uxmal + cenote | Uxmal + Kabah |
|---|---|---|
| Main attractions | 1 Maya city | 2 Maya cities |
| Swimming | In a cenote | In a cenote |
| Duration | 8–9 hours | 8–9 hours |
| Language | English, Spanish | English, Spanish |

## What makes Uxmal's architecture famous

UNESCO inscribed the Pre-Hispanic Town of Uxmal on the World Heritage List in 1996. Its monuments represent some of the finest achievements of Maya architecture: the facades feature geometric patterns, carvings and symbols, including images of the rain deity Chaac. The complexes at Uxmal and Kabah help explain how cities of the Puuc region developed.

During the excursion, look beyond the pyramid to the layout of the squares, the details of the stonework and the ornamentation. The more extensive itinerary provides an additional opportunity to compare the artistic traditions of Kabah and Uxmal. That is more rewarding than simply trying to see as many pyramids as possible without noticing their architectural differences.

## Preparing for your excursion day

Both routes involve walking around open archaeological sites. Bring water, a hat, sunscreen and comfortable footwear. Swimming conditions at the cenote depend on the particular site, including life-jacket requirements and areas open to swimmers. Do not assume that towels or any other equipment are included unless the programme explicitly says so.

Because both excursions take 8–9 hours, allow a full day. Avoid adding distant towns or late-night departures to the same schedule without allowing for travel time. Check current access to particular structures at Uxmal and to cenotes for the date of your visit.

For a broader itinerary across the peninsula, explore [Mexico tours](/mexico/tour/) and [cultural and historical journeys](/interests/culture-and-history/).

## Frequently asked questions about Uxmal excursions

### Which excursion includes Kabah?

[Uxmal, Kabah and cenote](/mexico/uxmal/uxmal-kabah-cenote-tour/) explicitly includes both archaeological complexes. Kabah is not listed in the [Uxmal and cenote itinerary](/mexico/uxmal/uxmal-cenote-tour/).

### Are admission tickets included?

The published descriptions of both excursions list admission to the main sites and the cenote. The exact tickets included depend on the excursion chosen.

### In what languages are the excursions conducted?

Both products list English and Spanish. Russian-language guiding is not promised without separate confirmation.

### Can I swim in a cenote?

Yes, swimming is included in both programmes. Access to the specific cenote and the actual conditions depend on the selected day and the site's rules.

## Uxmal and a cenote: Maya architecture and swimming in Yucatan

The [Uxmal and cenote excursion](/mexico/uxmal/uxmal-cenote-tour/) lets you explore one of Yucatan's most remarkable archaeological complexes and then relax by a natural pool, all in one day. The itinerary includes a visit to the ancient city of [Uxmal](/mexico/place/uxmal/) and swimming in a cenote.

**Duration: 8–9 hours**, starting at approximately **9:00–9:30**. Shared transportation, a certified **English- and Spanish-speaking** guide, and admission to Uxmal and the selected cenote are included. Meals, tips and personal expenses **are not included**.

## Uxmal: an ancient city on the Yucatan Peninsula

[Uxmal](/mexico/place/uxmal/) is one of the principal monuments of Maya civilisation. The city stands in Yucatan's historic Puuc region and is famous for architecture in which smooth lower facade sections contrast with richly ornamented upper levels.

According to UNESCO, Uxmal's most important structures were built mainly between the 7th and 10th centuries CE. Their facades feature geometric patterns, masks and images of the rain god Chaac. They show how the architecture combined structural solutions with religious symbolism.

Uxmal is recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Inscription on the list protects the monument; it does not grant unrestricted access to every wall and pyramid. Access is regulated by the archaeological site's staff.

## Pyramid of the Magician

One of the complex's most recognisable monuments is the **Pyramid of the Magician**, also known as the Pyramid of the Soothsayer. It is distinguished by its characteristic shape and position among the ancient city's other buildings.

The pyramid offers an insight into the way Maya architecture organised ceremonial space. At close range, visitors can make out the stone stairways, the volume of the buildings and their decorative details. A guide can explain how the complex changed during different phases of construction.

Present-day restrictions on access to individual structures may change. The excursion includes seeing the pyramid, but does not guarantee a climb to its summit.

## Governor's Palace and Nunnery Quadrangle

The **Governor's Palace** is known for its long facade and elaborate decoration. Its historical name should not automatically be read as an exact description of a modern system of government: archaeologists study the building's functions in the context of Maya society.

Another striking ensemble is the **Nunnery Quadrangle**. The name dates to the colonial period and does not establish that the complex was once a convent. Its buildings enclose a space with carefully worked facades and ornamentation.

These structures demonstrate why Uxmal is valued for its architectural details, not simply the height of its pyramids. Pay attention to the reliefs, recurring design elements and the relationships between the buildings and their rooms.

## What is a cenote, and why do people swim in one?

Cenotes are natural pools formed in the karst rock of the Yucatan Peninsula. Water collects in sinkholes and cavities in the limestone. Cenotes vary: some are open to the sky, while others are partly enclosed within caves.

In Maya culture, these water sources had practical and symbolic importance. Today many cenotes can be visited, although rules and facilities differ. Swimming may require a life jacket, a shower beforehand and compliance with restrictions on certain cosmetics.

The excursion includes **a visit to one cenote**. Depth, water colour, the presence of an underground cave and opening times depend on the particular site. These details are confirmed once the location is selected.

## Why swimming is a pleasant follow-up to archaeology

After walking among stone buildings and open squares, swimming offers a change of pace. This combination lets travellers experience two different sides of Yucatan: the historic setting of a Maya city and the peninsula's natural limestone landscape.

| Uxmal | Cenote |
|---|---|
| Pyramids and palaces | Natural pool |
| Maya architecture | Karst geology |
| Walking tour | Swimming subject to site rules |

However, the itinerary should not be assumed suitable for everyone without restrictions. The archaeological site can be hot, while cenotes may have slippery steps, deep water and specific entry arrangements. Those unable to swim should discuss access rules in advance.

## What to bring

For Uxmal, bring comfortable shoes, water, a hat and sun protection. For the cenote, pack swimwear and dry clothes to change into. Before swimming, check the rules on sunscreen and on storing belongings.

Allow enough time: **8–9 hours** covers not only two stops but also the transfers between them. Plan any lengthy evening activity on the same day with your return time in mind.

On the ["Viva Mexico" itinerary](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/), travellers visit Uxmal during their Yucatan journey. A standalone excursion can be convenient for visitors staying in [Merida](/mexico/place/merida/) or exploring the peninsula's archaeological monuments.

## Frequently asked questions about Uxmal and the cenote

### Is the cenote visit included?

Yes. Admission to the selected cenote is listed among the included services. The specific site is confirmed when the excursion is arranged.

### Is lunch included?

No. Meals are listed among the excluded services.

### How long does the programme last?

Approximately **8–9 hours**, departing between about 9:00 and 9:30.

### Can I climb the Pyramid of the Magician?

Access to individual structures is governed by Uxmal's conservation rules. Climbing the pyramid is not stated as an obligatory part of the excursion.

## Tours featuring the Uxmal and cenote excursion: choosing an itinerary

The ["Viva Mexico: Mexico City, Oaxaca and Yucatan in 12 Days" tour](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/) includes a dedicated day for the [Uxmal and cenote excursion](/mexico/uxmal/uxmal-cenote-tour/). The combination suits travellers who want to see outstanding Maya architecture without spending an entire day exclusively at an archaeological complex.

On this tour, the excursion takes place on **Day 10**, when the group is already in Yucatan. The overnight stay is in [Merida](/mexico/place/merida/). This is a full sightseeing day within a wider programme of several days exploring the peninsula.

## What Uxmal is like

[Uxmal](/mexico/place/uxmal/) is an ancient Maya city known for the Puuc region's architecture. Its buildings feature carefully worked stone, intricate ornamentation and rich symbolism. Major landmarks include the Pyramid of the Magician, Governor's Palace and the Nunnery Quadrangle.

Uxmal is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Much of the experience comes from walking through the archaeological zone: its facades and building layouts reveal how ceremony, politics and ideas about nature were interwoven in Maya culture. This day is especially rewarding for those interested in history and architecture.

After exploring the ruins, the excursion continues to a cenote. Yucatan's cenotes are natural pools in limestone rock, and swimming offers a break after a walk through the open-air archaeological site.

## How the excursion day unfolds

The standalone excursion is listed as lasting **8–9 hours**, with an approximate start **at 9:00–9:30**. It includes shared transportation, a certified bilingual guide and admission tickets to Uxmal and the cenote. Guiding languages are English and Spanish. Meals, tips and personal expenses are not included in the stated excursion-day services.

In practice, the day has two distinct parts. At Uxmal, visitors walk across an open site between stone structures; comfortable shoes, water and sun protection are useful. At the cenote, bring swimwear and a towel. The exact entry rules and swimming conditions need to be checked for the selected site and date.

## What the Viva Mexico itinerary adds

The [12-day tour](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/) begins in the capital, covering Mexico City, Teotihuacan and urban neighbourhoods. Oaxaca, archaeological monuments and craft villages follow. The Yucatan section includes Merida, Uxmal, cenotes and Chichen Itza.

The visit to Uxmal therefore marks a transition from central and southern Mexico to the Maya heritage of the peninsula. Afterwards, there is a separate day visiting the [Santa Barbara cenotes](/mexico/place/santa-barbara-cenotes/). The two days have different focuses: the first is mainly about a Maya city, while the second is devoted to natural pools.

When choosing, consider not only the excursion but also the overall trip length, the number of transfers and accommodation. The programme lasts 12 days, so it may be too long for a short holiday.

## How "Uxmal and Cenote" differs from "Uxmal, Kabah and Cenote"

The two excursions have similar names but different itineraries. [Uxmal and Cenote](/mexico/uxmal/uxmal-cenote-tour/) focuses on one archaeological city and a natural pool. [Uxmal, Kabah and Cenote Swimming](/mexico/uxmal/uxmal-kabah-cenote-tour/) adds a second Maya city, [Kabah](/mexico/place/kabah/), known for facades featuring masks of the rain god Chaac.

The second excursion is included in another multi-day product, the [8-day "Mexico Lindo" tour](/mexico/tour/mexico-lindo-eight-days/). Your choice depends on whether you prefer to spend more time at Uxmal or see two Puuc architectural sites in a single day.

## Frequently asked questions about tours including Uxmal and a cenote

### How long does the excursion take?

The standalone description gives a duration of 8–9 hours. That is one excursion day, not the duration of the multi-day tour.

### Is swimming in a cenote part of the itinerary?

Yes. Swimming is included in the description of the Uxmal and Cenote excursion. The specific pool's conditions and any restrictions for your chosen date must be confirmed.

### Which city is a convenient base for Uxmal?

On the Viva Mexico itinerary, the Uxmal excursion takes place while staying in Merida. Adding a visit to Kabah to the same day without changing the programme would not be appropriate.

### Is a Russian-speaking guide available?

English and Spanish are listed for this excursion. Russian-language guiding has not been confirmed in the published conditions.
